topic_title: Databricks: Agent Bricks, Unity Catalog & MLflow
sources: Databricks documentation, read 2026-10-03 through page summaries: 'Agent Bricks' (updated 2026-09-30: Knowledge Assistant, Supervisor Agent orchestrating Genie agents, agent endpoints, Unity Catalog functions, MCP servers and custom agents; custom agents in Python with LangGraph or LangChain deployable through Databricks Apps; foundation models; the Agent Bricks CLI and registering agents in Unity Catalog marked Beta; MLflow Tracing, evaluation and monitoring), 'Agent tools' (2026-09-11: Unity Catalog functions, MCP servers, retriever tools; EXECUTE permission; Unity Gateway control plane; on-behalf-of-user and service-principal invocation), 'AI Search' and 'Create and query an index' (2026-09-14; lessons 29 and 32), 'MLflow GenAI' (2026-09-21: tracing records inputs, outputs, steps, latency, tokens and costs; custom scorers, LLM judges and code checks; production monitoring scoring live traffic; traces and evaluations integrate with Unity Catalog), 'Service principals' (2026-09-11) and MLflow's GenAI evaluation documentation (lesson 46). NOTHING IN THIS LESSON WAS RUN ON AZURE OR DATABRICKS BY US: we have no accounts there and creating one is a step you must do yourself. Every platform statement is from the vendor page named, as read on the date given, and these products and their limits change quickly. The roadmap tells you to note any deprecated product (it records a Supervisor API deprecation); the Agent Bricks page we read lists a Supervisor Agent as current, so we cannot confirm what was deprecated: check the current release notes. Unverified: how Unity Catalog permissions map to each tool in your workspace (we read overview pages, not the privilege reference); the Beta features' stability.

sections.title: The Databricks agent stack
sections.body:
Databricks organises agent work around the **lakehouse** you met in lesson 32: governed data and tools in Unity Catalog, agents authored and deployed on the platform, and MLflow for tracing and evaluation. The Agent Bricks overview (updated 2026-09-30) lists:

| Piece | What it is (per the page) | Course link |
|---|---|---|
| **Knowledge Assistant** | A way to create domain-specific chatbots through an interface | Lesson 30 (RAG) |
| **Supervisor Agent** | Orchestrates multi-agent systems, coordinating Genie agents, agent endpoints, Unity Catalog functions, MCP servers and custom agents | Lessons 43 to 45 |
| **Custom agents** | Python agents in frameworks such as LangGraph or LangChain, deployed through Databricks Apps | Lessons 36, 37 |
| **Foundation models** | LLMs from several providers served through secure APIs | Lesson 7 |
| **MLflow Tracing, evaluation, monitoring** | Debugging, quality and cost measurement, production scoring | Lessons 46, 47 |
| **Agent Bricks CLI; registering agents in Unity Catalog** | Marked **Beta** | Treat as unstable |

And an AI Playground for prototyping a no-code agent before exporting it to code. The same distinction as on Azure applies: declarative, managed agents give less control; custom agents give your own loop and controls.

A product-name note: in lesson 29 we saw Databricks' vector service shown under the name AI Search (earlier Mosaic AI Vector Search), and this page now speaks of Agent Bricks. Names on this platform change; quote the page and the date, not the name from a course or a job advert.
sections.example: Fictional choice. The team wants a policy Q&A bot over governed documents quickly: a Knowledge Assistant. They also want the DataOps agent with approval gates in their own code: a custom agent on Databricks Apps, calling Unity Catalog functions as tools, with the gate in code.
sections.common_mistake: Treating a managed agent type as a governance solution. It speeds building; the approval, evaluation and identity design still need to be yours.
sections.check_question: Which Agent Bricks piece would you use for a custom approval gate in your own code, and which for a quick Q&A over documents?
sections.check_answer: A custom agent (Python on Databricks Apps) for the gate in your own code; a Knowledge Assistant for the quick document Q&A.

sections.title: Unity Catalog: who may do what
sections.body:
**Unity Catalog** is the governance layer. For agents the pages say:

- **Tools are governed objects.** Unity Catalog functions run custom Python or SQL logic, and agents can also use MCP servers and retriever tools. The documentation says tools require the **EXECUTE** permission to run; Unity Catalog enforces permissions and manages credentials, determining which data and tools users can access. A control plane ('Unity Gateway' in the page) controls access and monitors activity.
- **Identity of the call.** Tools can be invoked **on behalf of the user** (the agent acts with the user's identity, so it can reach only what the user can) or by a **service principal** (an identity for automation, assigned workspace roles and Unity Catalog permissions). This is lesson 51's delegated versus autonomous choice on this platform.
- **Data and indexes.** Tables and vector indexes are Unity Catalog objects. Lesson 32's constraint applies: the AI Search page says row-level and column-level permissions are not supported on an index, so per-user rules need separate indexes or an application filter.
- **Budgets.** Account-level, notify only (lesson 56).

The questions to ask, which become your criterion's explanation: *Which catalog, schema and objects does the agent read? Which principal runs it (user or service principal)? Which privileges does that principal hold (read on the table, EXECUTE on each function)? Where could a row-level rule be needed, and how is it enforced if the index cannot? Who may change the function definitions?* We did not read the privilege reference, so verify the exact privilege names and inheritance rules in the current documentation before you grant anything.
sections.example: Fictional. A retrieval agent reads a governed table of support-ticket summaries. It runs as a service principal with SELECT on that table only and EXECUTE on two functions. Because the index has no row-level permissions, regional teams get separate indexes, and the agent chooses the index from the caller's verified region.
sections.common_mistake: Granting a broad privilege on a whole catalog 'to get it working'. Grant on the specific objects the agent needs and nothing else.
sections.check_question: What permission lets an agent run a Unity Catalog function as a tool, and what are the two ways to choose the identity that calls it?
sections.check_answer: EXECUTE on the function. The call can run on behalf of the user (with the user's permissions) or as a service principal.

sections.title: MLflow: tracing, evaluation and monitoring
sections.body:
The MLflow GenAI page (2026-09-21) describes a loop: **instrument, observe, collect feedback, score, fix, evaluate, monitor.** Its parts map to lessons 46 and 47:

- **Tracing** records each agent run: inputs, outputs, intermediate steps, latency, token usage and cost. This is the trace of lesson 47, produced for you if you instrument the agent.
- **Evaluation** uses datasets (including ones curated from production failures) and **scorers**: custom ones, LLM judges and code checks. Lesson 46's advice stands: code checks where code can decide, judges calibrated against people where it cannot.
- **Production monitoring** scores live traffic to catch regressions and new problems, which is how a must-pass case becomes an alert (lesson 47).
- **Governed storage:** traces and evaluations integrate with Unity Catalog, alongside the organisation's data (so access control and retention from lesson 54 apply to them).

For your build, the criterion asks you to **build a small retrieval agent over a governed table, explain which Unity Catalog permissions apply and how MLflow evaluation is used, and note any deprecated product.** A plan that fits the Free Edition limits (serverless, quota-limited) uses only a small table:

1. Create a small Delta table of fictional runbook text with an access label (lesson 30's corpus works) in a catalog you own.
2. Create a retriever over it using the platform's AI Search or a Knowledge Assistant, or reuse your own lesson 30 code in a notebook if the managed feature is unavailable to you. Note which you used.
3. Wrap it as a tool the agent can call. Record the principal that runs it and its privileges.
4. Trace one run, and run your lesson 31 question set through MLflow evaluation with at least one code scorer and one LLM-judge scorer; calibrate the judge against 20 hand labels.
5. Write the permissions explanation, the evaluation results, and a deprecation note: list any product or feature you used or read about that the current docs mark Beta, preview or deprecated, with the page and date.
sections.example: Fictional deprecation note: 'Agent Bricks CLI and Unity Catalog agent registration: Beta per the Agent Bricks page dated 2026-09-30. Not used. The roadmap mentions a Supervisor API deprecation; the same page lists a Supervisor Agent as current; I could not reconcile them and will check the release notes.'
sections.common_mistake: Using a feature marked Beta as the foundation of a design without noting it. Mark every Beta or preview dependency and have a fallback.
sections.check_question: What does MLflow tracing record, and what are the two kinds of scorer?
sections.check_answer: Inputs, outputs, intermediate steps, latency, token use and cost for each run. Scorers can be LLM-based judges or code checks (custom ones allowed).

sections.title: Do it: lab
sections.body:
1. Create a small governed Delta table of fictional runbook text with an access label, in a catalog you own, in your Databricks workspace (Free Edition is fine; keep it tiny).
2. Build a small retrieval agent over it: a retriever as a tool, called by an agent. Say whether you used a managed feature or your own code from lesson 30, and why.
3. Write down the identity that runs the tool, the Unity Catalog privileges it holds (table and function), and what you would change if different users needed different rows.
4. Trace one run in MLflow. Run your 20-question set through MLflow evaluation with a code scorer and an LLM-judge scorer; calibrate the judge on 20 hand labels and report agreement and kappa.
5. Write the deprecation and status note: every Beta, preview or deprecated product you used or considered, with the page and date, and what you would do if it changed.

**Done when:** you have a small retrieval agent over a governed table, an explanation of the Unity Catalog permissions that apply, MLflow evaluation results with a calibrated judge, and a note of any Beta or deprecated products with page dates.

sections.title: Interview check
sections.body: Answer aloud first, then compare. Do not memorise the words; understand the shape.
sections.check_question: How do you build and govern an agent on Databricks?
sections.check_answer:
1. Data and tools are Unity Catalog objects; the agent runs as a named principal with only the privileges it needs: SELECT on the specific tables, EXECUTE on the specific functions.
2. Choose on-behalf-of-user when the agent should be limited to what the caller may see, and a service principal for autonomous work; know that vector indexes do not support row-level permissions, so I would separate indexes or filter in the application.
3. Build with a managed agent type for speed or a custom agent on Databricks Apps when I need my own controls, and keep approval gates in code.
4. MLflow for tracing, evaluation with code scorers and calibrated judges, and production monitoring.
5. Mark every Beta or deprecated feature with the date I read it.

sections.title: Evidence to keep
sections.body: Keep the table definition, the agent and tool, the privilege explanation, the trace, the evaluation results with judge calibration and the status note.
